title: Cambridge Study Reveals Why Some Smokers Get Cancer and Others Do Not
excerpt: A landmark Nature study finds that inherited genetics — not just environmental exposure — shapes how tumours evolve after DNA damage, offering the first direct evidence for a long-suspected link.
body:
• A University of Cambridge-led study published in Nature provides the first direct evidence that inherited genetic background determines how tumours arise and evolve after exposure to carcinogens such as tobacco smoke.
  • Researchers bred four strains of mice with varying cancer susceptibility, exposed them to the same carcinogen under identical conditions, then sequenced nearly 600 tumour genomes to track how each cancer developed.
  • While all tumours activated the same cancer-promoting signalling system (the MAPK pathway), the specific driver mutations and evolutionary paths differed dramatically based on each animal's inherited genetics.
  • The findings suggest that cancer screening, prevention and treatment strategies may need to be personalised based on a patient's genetic background, not just their environmental exposure history.

Scientists have found the first direct evidence that our inherited genetic makeup plays a powerful role in determining whether DNA damage from smoking, sunlight or other carcinogens leads to cancer — a discovery that could reshape how the disease is screened for and treated.

The research, published in Nature on July 27, was led by teams at the University of Cambridge, University of Edinburgh and institutions across Europe and the United States. It addresses one of cancer biology's most persistent puzzles: why most smokers never develop lung cancer, while some non-smokers do.

The Experiment That Removed Human Complexity

Proving the link between inherited genetics and cancer susceptibility has been notoriously difficult in human studies, because people differ in lifestyle, environment and exposure history. To eliminate these variables, the researchers designed an experiment with a level of control impossible in human populations.

They bred four strains of genetically diverse mice — spanning a range of genetic variation comparable to that found in human populations — and exposed every animal to a single, identical dose of diethylnitrosamine (DEN), a liver carcinogen found in tobacco smoke and some processed foods. Every mouse received the same dose at exactly 15 days of age under controlled laboratory conditions.

The team then sequenced the genomes of nearly 600 tumours that developed, analysed the gene activity within them, and reconstructed how each cancer evolved from its original mutation.

Same Endpoint, Different Paths

The results revealed a striking pattern. Across all mouse strains, cancers nearly always acquired a driver mutation that activated the MAPK pathway — a molecular signalling cascade that controls cell growth and is implicated in numerous cancer types. In that sense, the biological destination was the same.

But the route to that destination differed dramatically depending on the animal's inherited genetics. Different strains acquired different specific driver mutations, which in turn altered the activity of other cancer-associated signalling pathways. Some strains also showed a striking tendency for whole-genome duplication — an event where the entire set of chromosomes is doubled — while others did not.

"Cancer does not arise entirely by chance. Although tumours often reach the same biological endpoint, the path to that endpoint is determined by an individual's genetic background."

— Professor Duncan Odom, DKFZ German Cancer Research Centre, formerly at the Cancer Research UK Cambridge Institute

Implications for Precision Medicine

The findings carry direct implications for how cancer is approached clinically. If a patient's inherited genetics influences both whether they develop cancer and how their tumour evolves, then screening programmes designed around environmental risk factors alone may miss important populations — or over-screen others.

Similarly, the research suggests that responses to DNA-damaging cancer treatments could differ depending on a patient's background genetics, strengthening the argument for more tailored therapeutic approaches.

"If genetic background influences both cancer risk and the evolutionary trajectory of tumours, future cancer prevention and screening strategies will need to take into account inherited genetics and population diversity."

— Dr Sarah Aitken, Assistant Professor, Yale School of Medicine

Why This Matters for India and the Diaspora

India has among the highest rates of tobacco-related cancers globally, driven by widespread use of bidis, gutka and smokeless tobacco products. Understanding that genetic background — which varies across populations — shapes cancer susceptibility could be particularly relevant for India's diverse ethnic groups. The research points toward a future where cancer screening in Indian populations might be refined based on population-specific genetic risk profiles, rather than relying solely on exposure-based assessments designed for Western cohorts.

What's Next

The study was conducted in mice, and the researchers caution that more work is needed to understand what the findings mean for humans. The immediate next steps involve identifying which specific inherited genetic variants drive the differences observed and testing whether similar patterns hold in human cancer genomics data. Dr Sam Godfrey of Cancer Research UK noted that while the findings offer "a fascinating hint," translating them into clinical tools will require substantial further research. The study was funded by Cancer Research UK, the Medical Research Council, the European Research Council and Wellcome.
